$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the total deer population in the reserve, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=800$ deer, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(800-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{800-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{800-P} & =\int k\,dt \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|800-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $800-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$
Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}800-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 800-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 800-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =800-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial deer population affected by the parasite was $80$ animals. So, we apply the initial condition $P(0)=80,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0) & =80 \\ 800-K{e}^{0} & =80 \\ 800-K & =80 \\ K & =720\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=800-720{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $10$ days, the deer population affected by the parasite was $300$ animals. So, applying the condition $P(10)=300,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(10) & =300 \\ 800-720{e}^{-10k} & =300 \\ 500 & =720{e}^{-10k} \\ {e}^{-10k} & =\frac{500}{720}=\frac{25}{36} \\ -10k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{36}) \\ k & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{36})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when $600$ deer are affected by the parasite. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P({t}_{1}) & =600 \\ 800-720{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =600 \\ 200 & =720{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{200}{720}=\frac{5}{18} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{18}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{18}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that $600$ deer will be affected by the parasite after

$$

rounded to the nearest day.

$$

$$

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =3y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =3x-\frac{1}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨3y,\,3x-\frac{1}{y},\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨3,5,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨3y,\,3x-\frac{1}{y},\,-1⟩=⟨3,5,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3cy=3 \\ 3cx-\frac{c}{y}=5 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
3(1)y=3\,⟹\,y=1.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ and $y=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
3(1)x-\frac{1}{1}=5\,⟹\,x=2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=2$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\  & =3(2)(1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector  $v$ at $(2,1,6).$

Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 2v \\ 2u & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-2v\cdot 2u \\  & =-4uv-4uv \\  & =-8uv.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ -8uv & =0 \\ uv & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $uv=0$ defines the pair of intersecting lines $u=0$ and $v=0$ in the $uv$-plane. Notice that these lines correspond to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane.
